utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, whenever I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was difficult to find transport, but whenever I could go there I did. That's certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: When you stayed there, did you notice that he wore his military uniform?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Whenever he went to the line, he took his uniform with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. But did he also sleep in his uniform?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you that -- I don't really know. How would I know? He would come to have a rest, have a wash, and he would rest a little, relax.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: On the night of the 13th of September, did he sleep in his uniform?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't. I didn't see him in his uniform. When I came out of the room I said, Get dressed. He had some sort of a tracksuit on him and then he put something on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: What about the night before the killings? Was he sleeping in his military uniform on that night?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he slept in one room; I slept in another. As I mostly slept to the end of another room, whereas he was closer to the door; that was the situation. He was always ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: But what was he wearing when you first saw him after being woken up by the gunfire on the morning of the killings?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was in a tracksuit. He'd never prepared to sleep in the way he should have really slept. He would just have a little rest. He took his uniform off. He'd put civilian clothes on, but he could never fully relax as far as I could tell. As to what the child did during the night, I don't know. I didn't look into that really.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No. But you say that he was wearing a tracksuit on the morning when the shooting took place. What colour tracksuit was he wearing on the morning of the shooting -- just a minute. What colour tracksuit was he wearing on the morning the shooting took place?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: He would always sleep in his tracksuit. He couldn't fully relax. As to the colour of the tracksuit, I couldn't really say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Where did he put his weapon during the night when he was sleeping?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: He kept it with him, in his room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Did you see where he put the ammunition for that weapon?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: He had his own room, his own key. He said, Mom, don't be worried if they call me, if there's an attack of some kind. Don't be worried if I'm not in the room. And I believed my child, and that's what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: He told you that he had to be combat ready at all times, even when off duty. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And he had to be combat ready because he was guarding a front line that was a very short distance away. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And indeed your village of Kriz was effectively on the front line between the Bosnian forces and the battalion headquarters in the school at Cer. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. What do you mean? Could you clarify that question? There's something I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's okay. If there's any clarification to be done, the learned Prosecutor will do it. Did you ever see --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object to that at this point. The witness -- a question was asked and the witness was not able to answer it. She said, Yes, can you please clarify it. It's not for me to clarify a question that the Defence counsel asks that isn't answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Morrissey, you have to understand that the witness is not a military person, you know. Maybe the combat zone, the front line, are not familiar to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honour, if the Court thinks it should be clarified, I will clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Mrs. Stojanovic, the question I was asking you was this: That your village of Kriz stood between the front line where the soldiers were on guard and the battalion headquarters back in the village of Cer. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, apart from Janko's -- could I just ask you this: What kind of gun did your son, Janko, have with him?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I really know nothing about weapons. A rifle is a rifle. As far as I'm concerned, all rifles are the same; you use them to shoot and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Does the word Kalashnikov jog your memory as to what kind of weapon that your son had?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I knew nothing about such things. The only thing that was important for me was that they had something to eat, a warm room waiting for them. And as to what they had on them, what they would carry around with them, those are things I wasn't really interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, when you refer to "them," as you just did, are you speaking about your son, Janko, and his other friends who were doing the same job as him?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Including Mato?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Apart from Mato, who were the other young men from the village of Kriz who were in the HVO and performing duties from time to time?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was Janko and Marko Stojanovic, Mato Stojanovic, Pero Stojanovic; those are the sons of the Stojanovics. There was Josip Stojanovic, then there was Mijo Ratkic, Kazo Ratkic, Marto Ratkic, Niko Ratkic, the late Drago Ratkic, and there was another person, the late Marinko Stojanovic. They were from the village and they were all at the lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, you're in a position to say that your son, Janko, was not at the lines that morning, is that correct, because he was with you?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Because he had been at the line the previous day. On that day, he was on leave because you know there were shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And your understanding was that all of the young men would work in shifts, spending some time at the front line and then resting at their home in Kriz?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And your understanding was that those young men, all of them, had to be combat ready in case there was a battle at the lines or nearby. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Therefore, those young men all had to have their guns and ammunition with them. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's probably correct. But again, I can't say that for sure. I didn't go around with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, I understand that, Mrs. Stojanovic. But did you observe your own son Janko from time to time to have hand grenades or other military items with him?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't observe that. All I could see was his rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, on the night before the killings took place when you went to bed -- or before you went to bed, I'm sorry, did Janko tell you that there was a rumour that the Muslims might attack the next day?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. We could never have imagined such a thing because we were on good terms with them, on good neighbourly terms. Their children would pass through our villages and we were friends. I couldn't have imagined neighbours doing anything like that to us. I couldn't have imagined someone coming from the outside. I thought that if there was an attack they would go to the lines. If the troops arrived, we would flee. But that bloody morning arrived and they entered the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. But did your son tell you that there was the possibility of combat action in the general region of Uzdol before you went to bed the night before the killings?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't really remember. That night before, I didn't sleep. I was afraid because there were conflicts on a number of occasions, and we would flee and hide, but we thought there would be a truce and that things would calm down. So we thought that such things would not happen again. But that evening, as I didn't fall asleep in the evening -- well, from 12.00 I didn't really fall asleep. As to whether my son slept or not, I couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: What was it that you were worried by that caused you not to sleep? Was it the danger of firing and shooting and killing of people?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, I was afraid. I thought that he would come once his shift was over again, but that didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, you listed a number of young men before who were -- you said were involved in the HVO. And you said that they were at the lines. And I want to ask you: Are you able to be specific which of those young men were at the lines and which of those young men were on leave in the village on the morning when these killings took place?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. They had their own schedule. They had their own schedule behind the school, so I don't know who was there and who was at the lines. I can't just invent things now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No. Mrs. Stojanovic, did you become aware of any of the boys from the -- or any of the soldiers from the lines retreating and running back through the village of Kriz during the course of the morning?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I know nothing about that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, before I come to the fatal morning, I've got some questions about an institution called the home guard. Did you know what the home guard was?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what the home guard could have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of the home guard?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I have heard of the home guard, but I don't know what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, I won't ask you for an expert military opinion, of course. But in general terms you knew that older male citizens of the village were used by the HVO for local duties, such as patrolling crossroads and preventing the planting of land-mines. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I really know nothing about that. My house is a little on the outskirts of the village. I really couldn't move around a lot. I did what I had to do at home. Sometimes I would bake bread if the troops didn't receive bread; someone would collect it and take it away. I couldn't go to the stables and I really wasn't interested in such things. All I was interested in was whether my child would return alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Of course. But I have two questions arising from that. The first one is: In what circumstances would you bake bread for the troops in September of 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's something we did before. And from September 1993 onwards, I would only bake some bread for my child on occasion. But before -- when it was necessary, we would bake bread and prepare things for the troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And how long before these killings was the last time you had baked bread for the troops?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's okay. I don't need an exact answer, but was it a matter of days? A matter of weeks? A matter of months ago? What's your best recollection about that?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, a lot of time has passed since then, and I'm not 20 years old so I can't remember such things. It's difficult for me to remember what happened yesterday, let alone what happened 13 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, even so, I have to ask you to exercise your memory about matters. And one matter I want to ask you about is: Of the older male persons who still remained in the village of Kriz, which ones, to your knowledge, participated in the duties of the home guard?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't even remember what the home guard was and what they had to do. All I know about is these men that went to the lines and that's it. No one really turned to me. If they had orders of their own kind, they would go above the village and they would move around the fields. I don't know. I really don't remember these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Okay. I now wish to move to the morning of the -- of your flight and of the sad things that you saw. First of all, when you woke up, you could already hear gunfire taking place. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You got out of bed and you went to see where Janko was. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And you noticed him nearby. And I want to ask you: Precisely where was he when you first saw him?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when I got up it seemed as if the entire village had been affected because of the noise. It seems as if the entire village was being shelled. My child said, Mom, the village is on fire, run. I can't tell you anything other than what I have already said. I fled. I fell down. Now you're confusing me even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, there's no attempt to confuse you. I'm going to take you through very -- step by step, okay? Having got out of bed, you had the impression that the village was being shelled. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. You then saw your son Janko, and he was dressed like -- he was dressed like a civilian at that point. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Right. But even though he was dressed like a civilian, he had a combat rifle in his hand. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And he was shooting that combat rifle in his civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, when you saw him, he told you words to the effect: They are in the village. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, at this moment, you turned and went to your room to change your clothes in a hurry. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I didn't manage to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, I understand that. And what you say is that Janko told you: Hurry up. Run away. I'll cover you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'll protect you. He fired into the air from a flower bed. I fled and then everything that I have already told you about happened. I don't see why it's necessary for me to go over all of this again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You won't be taken to the discovery of the bodies again, but I need to ask you questions about your movements and what you saw. Now, from the time that you woke up until the time that you started to run, it was really a matter of about two minutes or so. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't have a watch on me, but it happened in a split second.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Of course. And when you ran, did you notice any smoke of any sort in the air outside your house?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Not at that point. I saw smoke when I was concealed in the bushes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, before you ran, did you hear Janko speaking to his friend Mato, Mato Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mato Stojanovic was in that other house, which I marked by number 2. He wanted to take the other door out and he saw his mother's dead body. Janko then told him to use the other window and not this way, and that was the last thing I heard before I fled. And I didn't see them again after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, I need to ask you some questions about that. At what point was it that you heard Janko and Mato speaking? Was that while you were in your room getting changed or was it before that time?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was after I had returned to get a change of clothes. I went across the room and I heard the voice say that that's what Janko was telling him. But after they had got out the window, I didn't see them again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you mentioned Mato seeing the body of his mother. Did you see the body of his mother at that time?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, where was the body of Mato's mother at that time?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was a bit further down from my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Did you see Mato at that time?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. They had two houses. The late Anica was in a different house with one of her sons, Ivan, and they were just across the road in a different house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I want to clarify this. At the time when you were still inside your own house, did you yourself see Mato or did you only hear him?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard Janko telling him to get out. It was later when I saw them again that I said, Did you see your mother? And he said, Yes, I tried to take the other door in order to get out. And he was grazed by a bullet or something and he was injured in his arm. That's what he told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, to your knowledge Mato was in the same position as your son Janko, that is to say, he was an HVO soldier --

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And when you saw him later, did you see him later that day or some days later on?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, not that day. It was several days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Are you aware of whether or not he was in military uniform at the time when he ran from his house?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. He said he had been wounded a little, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. You mentioned that -- I don't have your exact words noted here, but you mention that you heard a grenade or that you encountered a grenade going off in some form. Can you explain in what point that happened?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that. I'm not sure I even said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Do you remember any explosions during the time when you ran from your house up until the time when you fell down?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I heard sounds of shooting. Things were burning all around, but I didn't understand exactly what was happening. I'm not a military person and I didn't understand where the shooting was coming from. All I knew was that there was shooting all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. And that shooting was going on all over the place as you ran from the house in the way that you've drawn on the map. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but a little further down. The closest I heard was when I fell down to the ground next to the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, as you ran to escape you saw a man wearing a green uniform and a green beret. I want to ask --

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I want to ask you: Approximately how long did you have that man in view? Was it a matter of one or two seconds or ten seconds?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. You catch sight of something with the corner of your eye and you're terrified to death. It's a shock.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. You must understand there's no criticism implied of you at all in these questions, and I need your best answer that you can give now. Now, is your recollection now that you glanced at that man for about two seconds. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Not even that long probably. I just cast a sideways glance and turned my head immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And did he speak to you and say those words that he said to you, asking you to stop, before you looked at him or after you had already looked at him?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I looked at him and he said that, but I didn't get a good look. Before he stopped speaking, I was already on the run. I ran behind the house. There was a burst of fire. I thought that I would eventually get further, but when I heard the burst of gunfire go off, I just fell down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. The situation is that at the time you heard that burst of gunfire you had already gone around the corner of the house from that particular man?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. And at the time of that burst of gunfire, you couldn't see him. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, after that time you found yourself unable to move and you lay face down for a period of time that you're not sure about. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You then heard a conversation between individuals and I want to ask you: Did you look at or see any of the individuals who spoke later on, the ones who swore?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't see that. My eyes were closed and I was lying face down. How was I supposed to see anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Were you able to tell whether your son Janko was still shooting at that stage or were you simply able to hear gunfire from various places?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. He later told me that he had passed my body. He said, You were just lying there. You looked dead. I didn't dare touch you. And he followed the soldiers who were on their way further down the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: In that conversation when he told you about seeing your body on the side of the road, which soldiers did he tell you he was with? Running --

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When I was brought to Prozor, I didn't see my son there. He had been transferred to Split by this time. It was those others who told me, Is this you? You're still alive? And I said, Yes, I am. And then they said, Janko told us, My mother was dead. I saw her body lying there. I saw her body on the ground back in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And then luckily you went to see him in the hospital, is that correct, and he was alive?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I understand that you're only going on what you're told here and therefore it's hearsay evidence, but I just want to ask you what you were told. And that is: Who were the soldiers that your son ran away with down the road?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I know nothing about that. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Who were the boys you spoke to in Prozor about this?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I spoke to civilians in Prozor. Civilians, refugees who had arrived before I got there. I was the last to leave the village, but there were civilians who had left the village before me. There were other civilians at Kriz.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I think that becomes rumours, so I won't ask you any more questions about what you were told there.

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, look, you've nearly finished the questions here, and I thank you for the attention that you've given. As to the hill of Borak, what I want you to do is mark on a picture where that is, and I'll just endeavour to find the appropriate picture to show you and then I've finished. So just excuse me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Would Your Honours just excuse me. My numbering of the pictures, as you saw earlier on, unfortunately miscarried here. So we're just going to have to find the proper picture to show, and when we've found that we'll ... Okay. We think it's P321. Could the witness please be shown P321.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, I'm hoping I've selected the correct picture here. Does that picture allow you to see the hill Borak?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is Borak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Would you please draw a red line along where the hill of Borak is.

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where do you want me to draw this circle? Do you want me to draw a circle or mark it in another way?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Look, I think perhaps for our purposes the best thing to do would just be to draw a red X on the hill Borak.

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could you just -- and is it the fact that the village Kriz is immediately below that X?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to use letters?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY

utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I offer that --

utterances.text: Perhaps I should ask you one more question before I offer it. The hill Krstiste was a high hill, a tall hill, on --

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: There was a neighbour of mine, a big person, but he never called me granny. He always called me Zelenikusa. When I looked at him -- first I heard the voice and then I looked at him. I realised it wasn't him and then I fell down outside the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. So the person who you at first thought might be Mijo turned out to be the man in green. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.text: Ms. Stojanovic, in examination -- sorry, cross-examination, Mr. Morrissey asked you to mark on a photograph the location of Borak. utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown photograph 0299-2326.

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's a hill. That's opposite Borak.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Also, Mrs. Stojanovic, my learned colleague asked you at page 57: "Now, before you ran, did you hear Janko speaking to his friend Mato Stojanovic?" utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC

utterances.speaker: IVKA STOJANOVIC

utterances.speaker: MR. RE

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It's admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's exhibit P329.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I believe that there's no documents to tender from both parties. Yes. Well, Witness, thank you very much indeed for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. Madam Usher will show you out of the courtroom. We wish you a very pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, there's also the matter of the Karic depositions which has been put off over several different days, the argument for it. I've spoken to my learned colleague. I understand he's prepared already to argue it, or parts of it, this afternoon. Would it be appropriate after Ms. Chana's application?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, that depends on Mr. Morrissey's preparation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, yes, I've already flagged what the broad outline of what we say the point is. I'm happy to commence this afternoon and say what I have to say this afternoon. So I'm in the Chamber's hands, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Let me hear Ms. Chana first.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Can we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Now we are in open session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thanks, Your Honour. Well, Your Honours, the Defence submission is as indicated before, that the time has now come to play Mr. Karic's deposition in court. As I understand it, the power to grant a deposition hearing is a power to grant a reception -- a deposition for trial, for use at trial, so that the deposition, once ordered, becomes evidence unless it's excluded in some way under some other discretion. Now, in this case, the Prosecution proceeded at the time in a particular way according to the decisions taken. Questions were asked of Mr. Karic and the evidence in-chief was completed. Thereafter, cross-examination began. Cross-examination was -- was characterised by two relevant features. The first is that the cross-examiner indicated a reluctance to cross-examine. At the time he said he was -- he said he didn't have co-counsel, he wasn't familiar with the proceedings of the Tribunal, and that he was reluctant to cross-examine. But because of the health issues and because of what was seen at the time because as the protection of the interests of the accused, he was prevailed upon to cross-examine. It was asked whether he would be prepared to, and he ultimately took a decision that he was prepared to and he did so. So it has to be conceded that there has been some cross-examination upon this deposition already. When that cross-examination finished, there was some limited re-examination and then the matter terminated. But the other feature of cross-examination was that at the time the freedom to cross-examine by the -- by the then-counsel for Mr. Halilovic was subject to an objection by the Prosecutor who said that there should be no cross-examining pursuant to Rule 90, there should be no cross-examining outside of the scope of the evidence in-chief. And that objection, the presiding officer at the time did not rule upon herself but effectively reserved the question for a later time. Now, it seemed upon perusing that that what remains is that for the Defence to indicate whether they're happy with the cross-examination that they -- that we were allowed or whether we would seek to ask another question. It raises a difficult issue from the Defence point of view. Mr. Karic was very unwell back then, and the -- the indications that I have since that time are that he is -- he continues to be unwell. I'm not sure quite how -- how -- I don't have a medical opinion as to how he is right now, but I believe a medical opinion was sought concerning his illness, and I think our information is that it's quite grave. So the Prosecutor will probably have more up-to-date information than we do, but we did make an inquiry about his medical situation some time ago. I can't recall. I think it was during trial, though, and Mr. Mettraux will have it somewhere. I don't have it at my fingertips unfortunately. Your Honours, that's an issue. And therefore, I mean, considering whether you would grant our request to have further cross-examination, you have to take that into account and have some sensible, reliable information as to his health. That's a matter which I can't provide you with, his health status today. However, I can indicate that the further cross-examination the Defence wants to -- wants to engage in here is pretty narrow in scope. He was cross-examined quite fully about a number of matters and they were obviously relevant matters. But spectacularly missing from the questions was a question of whether he delivered any threats in the presence of his son or otherwise to persons in the village. And I just wanted to ask him that: Did you go to the village? Did you threaten the civilians? Or did you -- did you encourage the soldiers to deal with the civilians in a summary way and throw them into the Neretva? And if he says yes -- we anticipate he will say no. But if he says, Yes, I did actually make that terrible threat, well, then the next question will be of course: Was Sefer Halilovic standing nearby, and what did he say and so on? Now, it's evident from the questions that we've asked, the propositions that we've put to witnesses, the answers that we've elicited from some of those witnesses what the Defence position is about all of that and what we want to put to the Tribunal at the end. We are in a position of -- we don't want to concede that it shouldn't be put to Mr. Karic. In some respects -- the Defence wants to be clear as to what our case is, and it's not fair of us to say, Well, we don't want Mr. Karic to be called, we don't want to put that proposition to him. Of course we want to put that proposition to him because that's our case. It's the Defence case, which it always has been, that Mr. Halilovic was not at a meeting that -- at which Mr. Karic and Mr. Dzankovic and others certainly did attend in Grabovica on the 8th of September. But although we say Halilovic wasn't there, the Defence also takes the position that regardless of Halilovic being there or not being there, Karic never said anything like that at all, and that it's been -- the Defence case is that it's been made up for other reasons. And in that regard, Vehbija Karic ought to be given the chance to comment on that question and it would help the Tribunal if he did. All right, it's 12 years later, I accept, and, yes, he's in ill health, and yes -- although I'm not sure technically whether the Prosecutor would lead it or not, it must be blindingly clear that he would have been and I concede he was interviewed as a suspect. So all of those factors are relevant factors to take into account. But at the end of the day, that's the Defence case and I don't want to appear to -- frankly, I don't want appear manipulative and, you know, hiding behind something. We want to put it fair and square to that witness. And that's really why I want to have him made available for cross-examination for that limited matter. I don't seek to open up the matters on which he's already given evidence, even though clearly on the face of it there's some things we might want to ask further questions about. We think it's realistic given his health -- what we know about it at the moment; we might get further guidance from the Crown -- from the Prosecutors about that. But that's what we want. We want a limited cross-examination. If it needs to be on video, which I rather suspect it would have to be, then we will cooperate with any measure that has been taken. What we submit is that this matter could be dealt with really within minutes and not be too much of a stress for the witness, all other things being completed in an appropriate way. So therefore, our submission is as follows: That the deposition ought to be played to the Court, that after that the Defence be given a limited right to cross-examine on matters which -- on which they were effectively shut out on the previous occasion. The Defence doesn't have the right to re-open cross-examination on matters where we did cross-examine. And that the Prosecutor, I suppose, should they wish to clarify anything arising out of the new cross-examination, should be entitled to -- presuming it does arise directly out of cross-examination, should be entitled to ask any such question to clarify anything that should I should chance to leave vague in that regard. But the submission is that should happen. And I know about difficulties to arrange videolinks, and that's why we've harped on this subject a little bit, but we just don't want him to die, frankly, and it may be that that's a genuine possibility. We don't want the issue to be determined without him giving -- giving -- being given the chance to give that account. And that's our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any response, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution doesn't accept the argument that -- the fact that depositions are ordered and taken pursuant to Rule 71 automatically means that they become part of the trial record or that they are automatically tendered. I can give Your Honour a real practical distinction between this case -- at least another case in which I have been involved in in which depositions were taken, and that was the Simic, Tadic and Zaric trial, in which mid-trial during the Defence case the Trial Chamber ordered that depositions be taken in Belgrade. I think we took depositions from -- it might have been a dozen witnesses or so in Belgrade. But that was ordered by the Trial Chamber hearing it -- after having received the Defence 65 ter list and making a decision as to which evidence should be heard live and which evidence could be safely taken by deposition. And even then at the conclusion of that, about a month later, the Trial Chamber on a Prosecution application ordered two of those witnesses proprio motu to -- I think attend to give further evidence in The Hague on parts of their -- on parts of their evidence. So there's certainly a precedent within the Tribunal for deposition evidence to be supplemented by live oral testimony before the Trial Chamber, and of course by extension before the -- by videolink. And in the Simic case, the depositions weren't actually played to the Trial Chamber. It was a week -- six days of testimony. But they were received and admitted as a documentary exhibit. Another difference between that situation and this is that the depositions which were taken by videolink here, there were a number of exhibits actually tendered or -- which is a matter which the Trial Chamber has to determine, whereas in the Simic they were -- it was simply live -- or live deposition evidence. So the Prosecution's position up front is that the fact they were ordered doesn't mean they automatically go in. Especially in circumstances in which the request was made two years ago. The decision made by the Trial Chamber was two years ago and in very different circumstances with a very different witness list. The witness list was then over 100 and it's been dramatically pared back since. The Prosecution may not -- had it been in a position now, at the end of last year, considering its witnesses, may not have wished to call Mr. Karic at all. But that -- that's basically another matter. So we say that they shouldn't automatically go in. Now, we do of course concede -- well, it's not a matter of conceding. We acknowledge it was our application; it wasn't opposed by the Defence; and the Trial Chamber allowed the depositions to be taken, and quite extensively. The present Prosecution trial team does have some concerns about the manner in which the depositions were taken, and that is by no means the fault of the presiding officer, Ms. Featherstone. Her role was simply to preside. We do have some concerns about the way the questioning was conducted and some of the questions that were put to Mr. Karic at the time. And there are some matters which in the light of the evidence given before the trial, and if he was called by videolink tomorrow, we would be asking him some other matters, some slightly different matters. We would be asking to explore some other things that we say should have been explored with him if his evidence is to have its full probative weight and value before the Trial Chamber. In terms of the quality of the cross-examination, we don't disagree with Mr. Morrissey as to -- there are clearly some matters which the Defence -- which competent Defence counsel should and would have put to Mr. Karic at the time. And although he was -- he was represented -- the record shows the Defence counsel who was then in the matter -- his assignment was withdrawn by the Registry at a certain point. But having said that, the depositions go on for some 133 pages. Pages 89 to 128, 39 pages of those are actually the cross-examination of Mr. Karic. So there was a reasonable amount of cross-examination at the time. The Prosecution would, if the depositions are accepted into evidence, would -- we don't oppose Mr. Morrissey's application if it goes in for him to cross-examine further. We accept that as a matter of fairness he should be able to put the case as it now is at trial to Mr. Karic. However, if he's allowed to do that, the Prosecution similarly would request that if he can request questions, the Prosecution should also be allowed to ask further limited questions of Mr. Karic on matters which are relevant to the Prosecution case and the way it has been conducted at trial. The -- one of the matters Mr. Morrissey raised - and quite properly - was whether or not Mr. Karic made a threat -- or made the threatening gesture or said the words which some witnesses have said he said, and whether or not Mr. Halilovic was present. Now, I concede, and unfortunately I have to concede, that is something the Prosecutor should have asked Mr. Karic during the deposition evidence two years ago. And that question is properly a function of the Prosecution in-chief rather than the Defence in cross-examination. If it's part of our case, we should have put it before -- before the Trial Chamber in the depositions. We should have asked him: Did it occur and was Mr. Halilovic there and what happened? And in my submission it would be preferable to be asked in an open-ended manner for the witness to be given a chance to respond in his own words rather than in a cross-examining manner in which the cross-examiner would be entitled to put words in his mouth. Now, having said that, I don't know, having not spoken to Mr. Karic, what the answer will be. I suspect it will probably be as Mr. Morrissey has said. But it's certainly a matter which, in our respectful submission, should be a question which the Prosecutor puts and, if necessary, the Defence is entitled to cross-examine on that or any other relevant matters. In terms of the witness's health, we have contacted him. He is, of course, like most witnesses or many witnesses, reluctant, but he informs us that his health would permit him to give videolink testimony, if necessary, subject to medical supervision and breaks, of course. Now, I don't have any medical evidence which I can put before the Trial Chamber at the moment as to his current condition, but his condition was certainly outlined in the material supporting the Prosecution's application of March 2003, and we -- the date of that was the 14th of March, 2003, and we tendered the relevant medical material then. And if you look at that material, things haven't changed that much from what we have been told. So to summarise, we -- the Prosecution accepts that we ask for the evidence, and we're probably bound by that, although we say it's not automatic. And we do agree that the Defence should be allowed to cross-examine. But if they are allowed, we request the right to examine in-chief on a limited range of things which we can agree with the Defence about and put to the Trial Chamber and ask that if the depositions go in, the witness be ordered to provide further testimony by -- limited testimony by videolink with both parties allowed limited further examination. But that, of course, doesn't address the issue of any exhibits which were shown to him at the time and in particular his interview with the Prosecutor, which is MFI 2 on the application. Unless Your Honours wish to hear from me on that matter at the moment, which exhibits go in with him, those are my submissions on whether they should go in and, if so, on what conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Very concise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I will be, Your Honour. The Prosecutor should not be permitted to introduce new evidence from a witness at this late stage in the trial as a kind of condition attached to the introduction of this material and attached to cross-examination. The Prosecutor is not suggesting they have any right to this material at all, and that's right, they haven't. What's being submitted to you now is that you should allow the Prosecutor another attempt to elicit evidence in-chief from this witness, and there is no provision in my submission in the rules for that, and there is absolutely no provision, in my submission, in the rules for that. But more importantly there's no basis for doing it here. The Prosecution did have, as has been indicated, almost 100 pages of evidence in-chief. They made their decisions, and they really are stuck with them now. In any event, I'm going to put that proposition - it's a yes-or-no proposition - to this witness, if I'm permitted to, of course. And therefore, I'd submit that there is just absolutely no basis to start eliciting new material from this witness who has got a terminal cancer condition, it would appear, nearly 12 years later. That really just seems to be, in my submission, an attempt to get something extra, and I'd submit it shouldn't be permitted. May I say this: That in terms of exhibits that were tendered at the time, the record reveals what was put to the witness and what wasn't. And -- well, perhaps you can hear me about that another time as to what should happen with those exhibits. But it will be apparent that these documents that my friend has referred to were not put into the transcript in the least, and objection was taken to their translation and to their accuracy and so on like that. If we do descend to particulars about that, we might come up against one of our favourite investigators, Your Honours, so there will be a real live issue about that, but that's a matter that comes later on in my submission. So at this stage I've said what I've had to say on the current application, and we'll deal with the exhibits, depending on what Your Honours rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I forgot to say something in my response before, and that relates to the documents. There are a number of documents which have been shown to other witnesses -- not a number, there's a few, maybe half a dozen, which we would want to show to Mr. Karic if he is permitted to testify further and which really should have been shown to him at the time and in our submission would be highly relevant because he was a member of the inspection team and can shed light on those in the same way that Mr. Dzankovic could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe this issue is a very complicated one, and this Bench has to look into the history of all the proceedings of the deposition. And at this moment, we are not in the position to make a ruling on the spot. And we'll do so as early as feasible on that very issue. Are there any other matters that the parties would like to raise at this stage? I see none. So the hearing for today is adjourned.
